I hear your frustration, and I want to be honest with you: when it comes to the suffering of children, intellectual explanations often feel hollow or like "dodges" because no logical argument can take away the horror of that pain.

Based on Christian perspectives, there are a few different ways this is addressed, though they may not provide the immediate closure you're looking for:

*   **Human Freedom and Choice:** One perspective is that God gives human beings genuine freedom. This means that people can choose to corrupt what is good and commit evil acts. From this view, the suffering caused by abuse or violence is not God's fault, but the result of humans choosing to do evil (EveryStudent, [https://www.everystudent.com/forum/why-do-we-worship-god.html](https://www.everystudent.com/forum/why-do-we-worship-god.html)).
*   **A Broken World:** Another view is that we live in a world where sin and brokenness are systemic. Some suffering happens because of the choices of others, while some—like disease or accidents—happen simply because we live in a fallen world where laws of nature and biology can lead to tragedy (Sightline Ministry, [https://sightlineministry.org/daily-devo/hey-i-dont-deserve-this](https://sightlineministry.org/daily-devo/hey-i-dont-deserve-this)).
*   **God's Presence in Suffering:** Rather than providing a "why," some find the answer in the person of Jesus. The belief is that God did not remain distant from suffering but entered into it himself. By becoming human and suffering a "suffering beyond all comprehension," Jesus shows that God is not indifferent to pain but is "suffering with you" (thelife, [https://thelife.com/do-evil-and-suffering-disprove-the-existence-of-god-part-3](https://thelife.com/do-evil-and-suffering-disprove-the-existence-of-god-part-3)).
*   **The Promise of Justice:** Finally, there is the belief that while we may not understand why certain things are allowed now, God assures that everyone will eventually answer for their actions and that ultimate justice will be administered (EveryStudent, [https://www.everystudent.com/forum/why-do-we-worship-god.html](https://www.everystudent.com/forum/why-do-we-worship-god.html)).

I realize these answers are complex and may still feel unsatisfying. It is okay to feel rage or confusion when looking at the suffering of the innocent. If you're open to it, I'm happy to listen more to your thoughts or explore any of these points further.

It is completely understandable why this feels like a contradiction; it is often described as one of the most mysterious and confounding parts of the Christian faith (Cru, "Is Jesus God or Just a Good Man?").

When Christians speak about the Trinity, they are trying to describe a God who is more complex than we are, as He is spirit and not limited by the three-dimensional universe we live in (EveryStudent, "What is the Holy Trinity?"). Here is how they generally break it down:

**One in Essence, Three in Person**
The core idea is that there is only **one God**, but He eternally exists as **three distinct Persons**: the Father, the Son (Jesus), and the Holy Spirit (Cru, "Understanding the Trinity"). 

To help explain why this isn't a mathematical contradiction (like 1+1+1=3), some describe it more like 1x1x1=1 (EveryStudent, "What is the Holy Trinity?"). The distinction is made between "essence" and "person":
*   **Essence (or Being):** This refers to *what* God is. There is only one divine essence or "being," which means there is only one God (Cru, "Entender la Trinidad").
*   **Person:** This refers to *who* God is. The Father, Son, and Holy Spirit are distinct persons who have loved and interacted with each other for all eternity (Cru, "Is Jesus God or Just a Good Man?").

**Why they believe this**
Christians point to the Bible to support this view, noting that:
*   The Father is called God (Phil. 1:2), Jesus is called God (Titus 2:13), and the Holy Spirit is called God (Acts 5:3-4) (Cru, "Understanding the Trinity").
*   Yet, they are distinct: for example, the Father sent the Son into the world (John 3:16), and the Father and Son sent the Holy Spirit (John 14:26; Acts 2:33) (Cru, "Understanding the Trinity").

**Common Illustrations**
Because this is so hard to grasp, people often use analogies, though most admit these are imperfect:
*   **Water:** It can exist as ice, liquid, or steam—different forms, but all are the same substance, $H_2O$ (EveryStudent, "What is the Holy Trinity?"; EveryStudent — German, "Dreieinigkeit").
*   **The Sun:** It provides light, heat, and radiation—three distinct aspects, but only one sun (EveryStudent, "What is the Holy Trinity?").

Ultimately, many Christians acknowledge that human understanding is limited and that we cannot fully comprehend everything about how God exists (Cru, "Understanding the Trinity").

It is completely understandable why that sounds like a contradiction. It is one of the most mysterious and confounding doctrines in the Christian faith, and many people find it difficult to grasp (Cru, "Is Jesus God or Just a Good Man?").

To help make sense of it, theologians often distinguish between two words: **essence** and **person**.

*   **Essence (What God is):** This refers to God's "being" or "nature." Christians believe there is only one God in essence (Cru, "Understanding the Trinity: A Christian Core Belief"). Essentially, God is one single being (Cru, "Entender la Trinidad").
*   **Person (Who God is):** Within that one essence, there are three distinct Persons: the Father, the Son (Jesus), and the Holy Spirit (Cru, "Understanding the Trinity: A Christian Core Belief").

The reason it isn't considered a contradiction is that the "three" refers to the *Persons*, while the "one" refers to the *essence*. A contradiction would only exist if someone claimed God is three in the same way He is one (Cru, "Entender la Trinidad").

**How do the Persons differ?**
The Bible shows that these three Persons interact with one another. For example:
*   The Father sent the Son into the world (John 3:16), which means the Father and the Son are distinct Persons (Cru, "Understanding the Trinity: A Christian Core Belief").
*   The Father and the Son sent the Holy Spirit (John 14:26; Acts 2:33), showing the Spirit is also a distinct Person (Cru, "Understanding the Trinity: A Christian Core Belief").

**Common Illustrations**
Because this is so hard to wrap the human mind around, people often use analogies, though many scholars note that no human explanation is perfect (EveryStudent, "What is the Holy Trinity?"):
*   **Water (H2O):** It can exist as liquid, ice, or steam. The forms are different, but the essence (H2O) is the same (EveryStudent, "What is the Holy Trinity?").
*   **The Sun:** It provides light, heat, and radiation. These are three distinct aspects, but they all come from one single sun (EveryStudent, "What is the Holy Trinity?").
*   **Math:** Rather than thinking of it as $1 + 1 + 1 = 3$, some suggest thinking of it as $1 \times 1 \times 1 = 1$ (EveryStudent, "What is the Holy Trinity?").

Ultimately, Christians view this not as a math problem to be solved, but as a description of a God who is both one in nature and eternally relational within Himself (Cru, "Is Jesus God or Just a Good Man?").

It is a very common and important point of conversation. While both faiths revere Jesus, they understand his identity in fundamentally different ways.

From a Christian perspective, the response typically focuses on a few key points:

*   **More than a Prophet:** While Muslims view Jesus as a prophet, Christians believe that he is not only a prophet but also the Son of God and God in the flesh (Cru, [What Makes Christianity Different?](https://www.cru.org/us/en/train-and-grow/spiritual-growth/core-christian-beliefs/what-makes-christianity-different.html)).
*   **The Nature of "Son of God":** Christians explain that the term "Son of God" is not meant in a physical or biological sense, but in a spiritual one. They believe Jesus is the incarnate God, born miraculously through the Holy Spirit rather than a human relationship (EveryStudent — Slovak, [Ježiš v islame: podobnosti a rozdiely](https://everystudent.sk/jezis-v-islame)).
*   **The Purpose of His Coming:** A central part of the Christian answer is that God sent His Son not just to bring a message, but to provide a way for people to be reconciled with Him. This involves the belief that Jesus died for people's sins and rose from the dead—events that are fundamental to the Christian faith but are not accepted in Islam (Cru, [What Makes Christianity Different?](https://www.cru.org/us/en/train-and-grow/spiritual-growth/core-christian-beliefs/what-makes-christianity-different.html)).
*   **Fulfillment of Promise:** Christians often view Jesus as the "highest prophet" and the fulfillment of promises made by earlier prophets (like Isaiah) who predicted the coming of a Savior (EveryStudent — Slovak, [Ježiš v islame: podobnosti a rozdiely](https://everystudent.sk/jezis-v-islame)).

In short, while both agree Jesus was special and sent by God, Christians believe his identity as the Son of God is what allows him to bridge the gap between humanity and God.

While he didn't use those specific words, the texts highlight several instances where he made statements that his listeners understood as claims to be God:

*   **"I AM"**: In John 8:58, Jesus says, "before Abraham was born, I am!" This is noted as the same name God used when speaking to Moses from the burning bush (Jesus Film Project, [40 Interesting Facts about Jesus](https://www.jesusfilm.org/blog/jesus-facts)).
*   **Oneness with the Father**: In John 10:30, he states, "The Father and I are one" (Sightline Ministry, [Two Reasons Skeptics Believe Jesus is not God](https://sightlineministry.org/two-reasons-skeptics-believe-jesus-is-not-god)).
*   **Seeing the Father**: In John 14:9, he says, "Anyone who has seen me has seen the Father" (Sightline Ministry, [Two Reasons Skeptics Believe Jesus is not God](https://sightlineministry.org/two-reasons-skeptics-believe-jesus-is-not-god)).
*   **Direct Questioning**: During his trial in Mark 14:61-63, when asked if he was the Christ, the Son of the Blessed One (God), Jesus answered, "I am" (Cru, [Is Jesus God or Just a Good Man?](https://www.cru.org/us/en/how-to-know-god/is-jesus-god.html)).

The sources suggest that while Jesus often spoke indirectly or subtly about his nature, the people he was speaking to often interpreted these words as direct claims to divinity, sometimes reacting with anger or accusations of blasphemy (Cru, [Is Jesus God or Just a Good Man?](https://www.cru.org/us/en/how-to-know-god/is-jesus-god.html); Sightline Ministry, [Deity of Christ: True or False?](https://sightlineministry.org/deity-of-christ-true-or-false)).

It's a very common question, and it's understandable why your uncle would feel that way. When we think about something being copied and translated over thousands of years, it's natural to worry that the original meaning might have been lost like a game of "telephone."

However, based on historical and scholarly evidence, there are several reasons why many people believe the Bible remains reliable:

*   **An Abundance of Manuscripts:** While we don't have the original physical documents, we have a massive number of early copies (manuscripts). For example, there are nearly 25,000 handwritten copies of portions of the New Testament (EveryStudent, [Jesus in Islam](https://www.everystudent.com/wires/jesus-in-islam.html)). Having so many copies allows scholars to compare and cross-check them to reconstruct the original text with a very high degree of accuracy (Sightline Ministry, [Has the Bible Been Altered Over the Centuries?](https://sightlineministry.org/bible-altered-over-centuries)).
*   **High Consistency:** When historians compare these thousands of manuscripts, they have found that the New Testament is at least 99.5% accurate to the original (EveryStudent, [Jesus in Islam](https://www.everystudent.com/wires/jesus-in-islam.html)). The remaining 0.5% of differences are generally attributed to things like spelling or word order, which do not change the actual meaning of the text (EveryStudent, [Jesus in Islam](https://www.everystudent.com/wires/jesus-in-islam.html)).
*   **Direct Translation:** A common misconception is that the Bible was translated from one language to another, and then that translation was translated again, and so on. In reality, modern translations are typically made directly from the original Greek, Hebrew, and Aramaic languages based on those ancient manuscripts (EveryStudent — Vietnamese, [Các sách của Kinh Thánh - Lịch sử của Kinh Thánh](https://www.everyvietstudent.com/a/215KinhThanh.html)).
*   **Archaeological Evidence:** Findings like the Dead Sea Scrolls have shown that the biblical texts remained highly similar—nearly 100% identical—even over vast periods of time (EveryStudent, [Jesus in Islam](https://www.everystudent.com/wires/jesus-in-islam.html)).

In short, while human scribes did make occasional small errors, the sheer volume of early evidence allows scholars to identify those mistakes and be confident that the Bible we read today faithfully represents what was originally written (Sightline Ministry, [The Bible: How Big a Deal is Human Error?](https://sightlineministry.org/bible-human-error)).

The small differences that do exist are often just variations in spelling or minor things that do not change the actual meaning of the text (EveryStudent, [https://www.everystudent.com/wires/jesus-in-islam.html](httpshttps://www.everystudent.com/wires/jesus-in-islam.html)).
*   **Ancient discoveries:** Findings like the Dead Sea Scrolls have shown that even when comparing modern Bibles to much older texts, they remain nearly 100% identical (EveryStudent, [https://www.everystudent.com/wires/jesus-in-islam.html](httpshttps://www.everystudent.com/wires/jesus-in-islam.html)).

In short, while humans certainly made small mistakes while copying, the massive amount of evidence available allows scholars to identify those mistakes and maintain a very high level of confidence in the original message.

I hope that helps provide some perspective! It’s a deep topic, and it's okay to keep exploring it.

It’s completely understandable that those terms might sound unfamiliar if you didn't grow up in an Orthodox household. 

While the specific term "Theotokos" isn't defined in the provided texts, I can help clarify the broader context of Christian beliefs and how different groups relate to one another.

### What is "Theotokos"?
Though the provided documents do not explicitly define "Theotokos," in a Greek Orthodox context, it is a title for Mary, the mother of Jesus. It is a Greek term that translates to "God-bearer" or "the one who gave birth to God." This title is closely tied to the belief in the **Virgin Birth**, which is a core part of the Christian faith.

According to the *Apostles' Creed* (an early creed of the Christian faith), it is affirmed that Jesus Christ "was conceived by the Holy Spirit, born of the virgin Mary" (Sightline Ministry, [https://sightlineministry.org/jesus-virgin-birth](https://sightlineministry.org/jesus-virgin-birth)).

### Do all Christians believe it?
Christianity is composed of many different denominations—including Catholic, Orthodox, Evangelical, Pentecostal, and Methodist—and while they share core foundations, they do have theological differences (EveryStudent — Greek, [http://www.everystudent.gr/a/difference.shtml](http://www.everystudent.gr/a/difference.shtml)).

Here is how Christians generally align:

*   **Core Agreements:** Most Christians agree on several fundamental truths: that Jesus is the Son of God, that He died on the cross and was resurrected, and that the Gospel is "Good News" (Sightline Ministry, [https://sightlineministry.org/five-misconceptions-of-christians](https://sightlineministry.org/five-misconceptions-of-christians)).
*   **The Virgin Birth:** The belief in the miraculous conception of Jesus by the Holy Spirit is a widely held belief, as seen in the Apostles' Creed (Sightline Ministry, [https://sightlineministry.org/jesus-virgin-birth](https://sightlineministry.org/jesus-virgin-birth)).
*   **Theological Differences:** While there is a shared foundation, "there are plenty of theological disagreements to go around" among different Christian groups (Sightline Ministry, [https://sightlineministry.org/five-misconceptions-of-christians](https://sightlineministry.org/five-misconceptions-of-christians)).

In short, while the specific emphasis or way the title "Theotokos" is used might vary between a Greek Orthodox family and, for example, an Evangelical church, the underlying belief in the unique, miraculous nature of Jesus' birth is a central thread that connects many Christians.
